paras: The Wilmington mobbing of John H. Harris was the pursuit of a Black Democratic campaign speaker from Virginia by a crowd through the streets of Wilmington, Delaware, on the evening of August 3, 1880, after he spoke at City Hall. Policemen met him and escorted him to the railroad depot, and no injury to him was reported. Democratic papers as far away as Texas and Kentucky retold it as Republicans denying free speech to a Black Democrat.

Harris, described as "the colored Democrat hailing from Virginia," was speaking in Delaware for the Democratic presidential ticket of Hancock and English in the 1880 campaign. The Saturday before, he had been stoned while trying to speak at New Castle and had sought the protection of the sheriff. At City Hall he told his audience he had heard that a party of 300 in town proposed to mob him if he took the platform.

According to the Wilmington Every Evening, as reprinted in the Richmond Dispatch, Harris spoke for about an hour to a mixed crowd that jeered and laughed, and his call for cheers for Hancock and English drew no response. Outside, a party of white men, some of them members of the Young Men's Republican Club, talked of rotten-egging him, and when he came out he was surrounded so closely that he could hardly move. After a stop in a restaurant he was surrounded again, until at Fourth street a man named Ned Leary took him into the Swan Hotel, from which he slipped out the back onto Shipley street.

The crowd, which the paper said was made up of whites and Blacks and included members of the Lincoln Republican Club, ran after him down Shipley street, some carrying heavy sticks and shouting "After him," "Run him out," and "Knock him on the head." A little below Third street Harris met Sergeant Whelan and four officers, who formed a guard and walked him to the depot while the crowd followed. The Every Evening judged that the mob's chief object was to run him out of town, but that he would probably have been hurt had he headed toward the outskirts. Instead of taking a train, it reported, he slipped away from the depot with a white friend and reappeared in the city the next morning.
No arrests are reported; two days later the Wilmington Daily Gazette wrote that Harris had been "threatened and hooted at and mobbed in this city" and blamed the Republican party.

The fullest account came from the Every Evening, which the Richmond Daily Dispatch reprinted on August 6 under the headline "A Colored Virginia Democrat Abroad" with a deck saying he was hooted, jeered and pursued to the train by a crowd of blacks and whites. That account mixed ridicule of the speech as "rambling" with a detailed, partly comic narrative of the chase, while still calling the pursuers a mob that would have injured him. A shorter version from the Baltimore Sun, reprinted by the New York Sun as "Maltreating a Democratic Negro" and paraphrased by the Bel Air Aegis & Intelligencer, described the pursuers only as "colored men."

Democratic papers used the episode as a partisan answer to reports of Southern outrages. The Aegis called the New Castle stoning "another case of Ku Kluxing" on "the wrong side," the Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman predicted the mobbing would "escape the notice of the stalwart press," and the Hickman Courier blamed "a mob of black and white Republicans." Every report found appeared in white newspapers, and no Black-press account of the episode was found.

Accounts differ on who chased Harris: the Every Evening described a crowd of whites and Blacks and named two Republican clubs among the whites, while the Baltimore Sun version spoke only of "an excited crowd of colored men." The Sun version also said the crowd caught Harris and that he left on the first train, whereas the Every Evening did not say he was seized and reported that he stayed in the city. As the local paper, and the one that reported his reappearance the next morning, the Every Evening is the better evidence on whether he left town.

reader.title: Wilmington mobbing of John H. Harris
bases: A crowd surrounded and chased Harris through the streets with sticks and threats until police escorted him away; no blows or injuries are reported in Wilmington (A7, A9, A13).

The Wilmington Every Evening account (A7) and the separately written Baltimore Sun version (A9, A8) and a Kentucky brief (A13) agree that a crowd pursued Harris after his City Hall speech and police escorted him to the depot, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: Wilmington Every Evening (via Richmond Dispatch)
accounts.gist: A mixed crowd of whites and Blacks, including Republican club members, surrounded and chased Harris with sticks and threats; police escorted him to the depot, but he eluded the crowd and stayed in the city.

accounts.label: Baltimore Sun (via New York Sun and Bel Air Aegis)
accounts.gist: An excited crowd of colored men pursued and caught Harris; he broke loose, was protected by police, escorted to the depot and took the first train.

accounts.label: Hickman Courier brief
accounts.gist: A mob of black and white Republicans chased him around town; a posse of police protected him from violence.

framing.detail: The Every Evening reprint headlined 'A Colored Virginia Democrat Abroad', called the speech 'rambling' but described the crowd as a 'mob' that would have injured him.
The New York Sun's headline 'Maltreating a Democratic Negro' and the Aegis's 'another case of Ku Kluxing' framed it as Republican-side violence.
Democratic papers in Wilmington, Texas and Kentucky blamed Republicans and expected the 'stalwart press' to ignore it.
